newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: North Korean meet nets $282 mln in foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: North Korean meet nets $282 mln in foreign investment.

text.p: Reclusive North Korea's biggest experiment with capitalism bore its first fruit on Sunday as foreign businessmen clinched US $282 million in deals with the isolated Stalinist state.

The agreements ranged from hotels to motorcycle plants and could be followed by announcements of pacts worth hundreds of millions more when a historic three-day investment forum concludes on Sunday with a late afternoon news conference.

North Korea, which has sneered at the capitalist world for decades, is hoping to create a 750 sq km (280 sq mile) free trade zone in its northeast and attract enough foreign investors to help revive its teetering economy.

Confirmed deals included a $180 million plan by the Emperor Group of Hong Kong to build a five-star hotel on the coast near Rajin. The group would invest an additional $30 million in a banking venture, a North Korean official said.

An overseas Korean conglomerate, as yet unidentified, committed $50 million to build a hospital and China's Yantai Motorcycle Co will build a $5 million motorcycle plant in the special zone, the official said.

Thailand's Loxley Group agreed to invest $10 million in a project to build prefabricated housing and upgrade telecommunications system in Rajin-Sonbong located in the northeast corner of North Korea near the Chinese border.
Observers at the forum said negotiations for a joint venture flour mill with the bordering Chinese province of Yangi and talks for an oil refinery were also likely to yield deals.
Yangi province was also said to be discussing a deal for a bottling plant and an plastic factory, while Hong Kong and overseas Korean concerns were focusing on a five-star hotel.
The Japanese city of Niigata and China's Jilin province were also poised on Sunday to sign an agreement to provide some level of infrastructure support for the zone, officials said.
"There are definitely things happening here, it's just a matter of what people do after the forum rather than what they say here," said an economic researcher from the United States.

North Korea's first attempt at linking up with capitalism has attracted 550 businessmen and reporters who joined North Korean officials for seminars on tourism, banking, agriculture, electronics manufacturing and infrastructure development.
North Korea, eager to impress its guests, built a gleaming new conference centre in the middle of the free trade zone on the Tumen River border region with China and Russia.

North Korean officials quickly got down to business. With the paint still wet on the new building, the chairman of the Committee for Promotion of External Economic Cooperation. appealed for billions of dollars of investment.
Kim Jong-u painted a picture of a free trade zone with low taxes, visa-free travel, high-tech infrastructure and laws governing investment.

The omnipresent "guides" shadowing guests eventually relaxed enough to allow foreigners to walk freely in Rajin and Sonbong cities. Businessmen and researchers were seen wandering into residential neighborhoods, much to the surprise of residents.
Outside urban areas, Rajin-Songong appeared desolate, with only one village visible on the 50 km (30 mile) drive to the Chinese border to the north.

During the hour-long journey, visitors saw only two cargo trucks on the road which serves as an overland shipping route for goods from Ragjin Sonbong to Yangi Province. The goods originate in Pusan, South Korea, with which North Korea is still technically at war, and are brought to Ragjin Sonbong by boat.
